reference.source: Textbook of Pediatric Rheumatology / ILAR & PRINTO criteria
clinicalPearls: A chronic autoimmune exocrinopathy targeting salivary and lacrimal glands, but children often present differently from adults
Recurrent bilateral parotid gland swelling (parotitis) is a common and sometimes presenting feature in children, more so than the classic sicca symptoms
Dry eyes and dry mouth (sicca) may be underreported by children, so a low threshold for objective testing is needed
Extraglandular manifestations include arthralgia, arthritis, renal tubular acidosis, cytopenias and neurological involvement
Anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB antibodies, antinuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinaemia support the diagnosis
There is a long-term, though low in childhood, risk of B-cell lymphoma, warranting attention to persistent glandular enlargement
Management is largely supportive for sicca symptoms, with immunosuppression reserved for significant systemic involvement
reference.pathophysiology: Juvenile Sjogren syndrome is characterised by lymphocytic infiltration of exocrine glands, chiefly the salivary and lacrimal glands, driven by autoreactive T and B cells. Glandular epithelial activation, type I interferon signalling and B-cell hyperactivity lead to progressive glandular dysfunction and the production of autoantibodies such as anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB. Chronic B-cell stimulation underlies the hypergammaglobulinaemia and the long-term predisposition to lymphoma, while immune complex and interferon-driven inflammation account for extraglandular features affecting joints, kidneys, blood and the nervous system.
additionalDifferentials: Viral parotitis (e.g. mumps, Epstein-Barr virus, HIV) and other infective sialadenitis
Systemic lupus erythematosus and other overlapping connective tissue disease
additionalInvestigations: Anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB antibodies, antinuclear antibody and rheumatoid factor
Immunoglobulin levels looking for polyclonal hypergammaglobulinaemia
Objective ocular testing (e.g. Schirmer test and ocular surface staining)
Salivary gland ultrasound and, where indicated, minor salivary gland biopsy
Renal function and urinalysis to detect tubular acidosis
redFlags: Persistent unilateral or hard glandular enlargement raising concern for lymphoma
Renal tubular acidosis with electrolyte disturbance
Neurological involvement such as myelopathy or neuropathy
reference.prognosis: Childhood disease is often dominated by recurrent parotitis and may follow a relatively indolent glandular course, but systemic involvement and the lifelong, if low, lymphoma risk require ongoing surveillance. Sicca symptoms tend to persist and can affect dental and ocular health over time.
pitfalls: Attributing recurrent parotid swelling to simple infection and missing the underlying autoimmune process
Relying on adult sicca-based criteria when children present with glandular swelling instead
Overlooking renal tubular acidosis and its metabolic consequences
Neglecting dental and ocular preventive care
Failing to investigate persistent asymmetrical glandular enlargement for lymphoma
references: Proposed criteria for childhood Sjogren syndrome
ACR-EULAR classification criteria for Sjogren syndrome
